(Coastal Living) -- The Little Dipper's seven patio tables overlook a twinkling Caribbean. Tonight, the chef -- who's also waiter and hostess -- prepares Creole fish with vegetables. Although the small restaurant is one of the best in Grenada, it's the vista that stands out. Founded in the late 17th century, the capital city of St. George's sits on the island's southwest coast. Sailboats sway at anchor on Clarkes Court Bay, and lights blink on against dark green hills. The island's hidden treasure is its views -- and not just from quaint seaside cafés. Take the nearby resort of Laluna, on Portici Bay. With 16 hillside cottages huddled around a private cove beach, it overflows with scenic panoramas. Founded by a former fashion consultant from Italy, Laluna is chic, but not pretentious -- a stylish retreat on one of the Caribbean's quietest islands. Eco-inspired rooms feature fabric-draped four-poster beds from Bali, individual plunge pools, and bamboo-topped verandas. The most distant cottage sits 150 feet from the beach, making the resort a barefoot, lounging kind of place. Ultracasual dress code aside, Laluna takes meals seriously. Dinner comes prepared by an Italian chef who mingles his home country's techniques with Caribbean flavors. You can start with octopus salad with potatoes and chickpeas, then make your way down the menu to pappardelle with a nutmeg cream sauce. It won't be the last time you see nutmeg on a menu here. Grenada provides a third of the world's supply of the spice, which can be sampled as a powder, syrup, or jam. Almost every visitor brings some home, usually in a small basket also packed with cloves, cinnamon, mace, bay leaves, and ginger. It takes a lush climate, such as the rain forest at Grenada's center, to produce these flavors. Grand Etang National Park preserves the island's tropical flora and fauna. Visitors can book guides to lead them through terraced banana farms and forests of giant gommier trees, teak, and wild orchids. From a mountain peak, 90 percent of the island is visible, vivid green after a midday rain. As one might expect, the cities here move at a sleepy, island pace. But the township of Gouyave on Grenada's western coast jumps to life on Fish Fridays, which are part street-food festival, part outdoor concert, and part extended-family gathering. Beginning late afternoon, the fishing village's streets and side passages fill with tables of seafood. Vendors sell sample-size servings of everything from lobster to jerked marlin to deep-fried fish cakes. Music lifts the spirit, as do the enthusiastic greetings of friends and relatives. Visitors to Gouyave are a little reluctant to leave. But eventually they'll head back to Laluna, along a cliffside road illuminated by stars on a cloudless night -- yet another unforgettable view. Island Info . Laluna's cliffside cottages start at $390. Rates do not include meals, but all snorkeling and kayaking is included; 866/452-5862 or laluna.com. Guided hikes from Henry's Safari Tours cost $40 to $55 per person. Denis Henry offers trips tailored to your experience level. His taxi tours are also the best on the island; 347/721-9271 or henrysafari.com. Reservations at Little Dipper on Clarkes Court Bay in Woburn can be made through Laluna, or by calling 473/444-5136. From Laluna, a round-trip taxi to Fish Fridays in Gouyave costs roughly $100. Food at the festival will run between $15 and $20 per person. # Grenada: The Caribbean's Hidden Spice Island

*(Coastal Living)* -- The Little Dipper's seven patio tables gaze out over a shimmering Caribbean sea. Tonight, the chef—who doubles as waiter and hostess—prepares Creole fish with vegetables. Though this intimate restaurant ranks among Grenada's finest, it is the view that truly commands attention. Founded in the late 17th century, the capital city of St. George's rests along the island's southwest coast, where sailboats drift at anchor in Clarkes Court Bay and lights flicker to life against darkening green hills. Grenada's greatest treasure lies in its vistas—found not only at charming seaside cafés, but throughout the island.

Consider the nearby resort of Laluna, perched above Portici Bay. With sixteen hillside cottages clustered around a private cove beach, the property offers scenic panoramas at every turn. Founded by a former Italian fashion consultant, Laluna exudes chic sophistication without pretension—a stylish sanctuary on one of the Caribbean's most tranquil islands. Its eco-inspired accommodations feature fabric-draped four-poster beds from Bali, private plunge pools, and bamboo-topped verandas. The farthest cottage sits just 150 feet from the shore, cultivating an unhurried, barefoot ambiance throughout the resort.

Despite its relaxed dress code, Laluna approaches dining with genuine dedication. Each evening, an Italian chef crafts meals that blend techniques from his homeland with Caribbean flavors—perhaps beginning with an octopus salad accented by potatoes and chickpeas, then progressing to pappardelle bathed in a nutmeg cream sauce. This will not be your last encounter with nutmeg here: Grenada supplies a third of the world's nutmeg, available in forms ranging from powder to syrup to jam. Nearly every visitor departs with a sampling, typically nestled in a small basket alongside cloves, cinnamon, mace, bay leaves, and ginger. While Grenada boasts no glittering casinos or towering resorts, it cultivates more spices per square mile than anywhere else on Earth.

*Coastal Living: The Other Caribbean*

Such abundance demands a lush climate—one found at the island's rainforest heart. Grand Etang National Park safeguards Grenada's tropical flora and fauna, and visitors can arrange guided treks through terraced banana farms and forests brimming with towering gommier trees, teak, and wild orchids. From a mountain summit, nearly ninety percent of the island unfolds before you, its verdant hues intensified after a midday rain.

As one might expect, Grenada's towns generally embrace an unhurried, island rhythm. Yet the western coastal town of Gouyave springs to vibrant life each Fish Friday—an event part street-food festival, part outdoor concert, part extended family reunion. Beginning in late afternoon, the fishing village's streets and alleyways fill with tables laden with seafood, as vendors offer sample portions of everything from lobster to jerked marlin to crisp fish cakes. Music fills the air, matched only by the warmth of friends and relatives greeting one another.

Visitors to Gouyave often find themselves reluctant to depart. Eventually, though, they return to Laluna along a cliffside road illuminated by stars on a clear night—one more unforgettable view to close the evening.

---

**Island Info**

Laluna's cliffside cottages begin at $390 per night. Rates exclude meals but include snorkeling and kayaking; call 866/452-5862 or visit laluna.com.

Guided hikes through Henry's Safari Tours range from $40 to $55 per person, with trips tailored to your experience level. Denis Henry also offers the island's premier taxi tours; call 347/721-9271 or visit henrysafari.com.

Reservations at Little Dipper, located on Clarkes Court Bay in Woburn, can be arranged through Laluna or by calling 473/444-5136.

From Laluna, round-trip taxi service to Fish Fridays in Gouyave costs approximately $100, with festival fare running between $15 and $20 per person.

# Discovering Grenada: Where Natural Beauty Meets Culinary Artistry

Nestled along the Caribbean coastline, the Little Dipper restaurant offers a mesmerizing showcase of Grenada's natural splendor. Guests seated at the patio tables are treated to sweeping views of the twinkling Caribbean Sea, with the historic capital of St. George's providing a picturesque backdrop. The interplay of shimmering water, colonial architecture, and vibrant evening lights creates an atmosphere that feels both timeless and enchanting—a perfect introduction to what makes this island nation so special.

## A Landscape of Hidden Treasures

What truly sets Grenada apart is the accessibility of its breathtaking scenery. Unlike destinations where stunning views are reserved exclusively for luxury travelers, Grenada's natural beauty welcomes everyone. Whether you're enjoying a casual meal at a humble seaside café or indulging in the sophisticated ambiance of an upscale resort like Laluna on Portici Bay, the island's dramatic coastlines and lush landscapes remain a constant, democratic gift to all who visit. This blend of accessibility and grandeur is perhaps Grenada's best-kept secret.

## Laluna: Understated Luxury on Portici Bay

Among Grenada's premier accommodations, Laluna stands out for its distinctive approach to luxury—one that favors authenticity over ostentation. The resort features eco-inspired hillside cottages that blend seamlessly into the natural terrain, each offering guests the indulgence of a private plunge pool. Rather than cultivating a stuffy, formal atmosphere, Laluna embraces a barefoot, relaxed philosophy that puts guests at ease. Just steps away from the beach, the resort strikes a delicate balance: chic enough to feel special, yet unpretentious enough to feel like a genuine escape from the everyday world.

## A Culinary Journey Through Fusion Cuisine

The dining experience at Laluna reflects this same thoughtful balance, marrying Italian culinary traditions with the vibrant flavors of the Caribbean. This fusion approach yields dishes that surprise and delight the palate—from a delicately prepared octopus salad that highlights fresh, local seafood, to nutmeg cream pappardelle, a pasta dish that ingeniously incorporates one of Grenada's signature spices into a classic Italian preparation. Each plate tells a story of cultural exchange, honoring both the technical precision of Italian cooking and the bold, aromatic character of Caribbean ingredients.

## The Spice Island's Aromatic Legacy

Grenada's culinary identity is inextricably linked to its extraordinary spice production. The island has earned global recognition for producing approximately one-third of the world's nutmeg supply, a remarkable feat for a nation of its size. Even more impressive is Grenada's distinction as home to the highest concentration of spice cultivation per square mile anywhere on Earth. This agricultural abundance is no accident—it's the direct result of the island's lush rainforest climate, which provides the ideal conditions for nutmeg, along with other spices, to flourish. This rich botanical heritage has earned Grenada its well-deserved nickname: the "Spice Island," a title that resonates throughout its cuisine, culture, and identity as a Caribbean destination.

# Grenada: The Spice Isle's Quiet Allure

Tucked away in the southeastern Caribbean, Grenada offers travelers a refreshing departure from the region's more crowded, commercialized destinations. This island nation has cultivated a reputation for understated charm, where authentic experiences take precedence over flashy tourist traps.

## Seaside Dining with Soul

Grenada's culinary scene shines through intimate, unpretentious venues rather than sprawling resort complexes. The Little Dipper exemplifies this approach—a beachside restaurant where diners can enjoy fresh, locally-sourced meals with their toes practically in the sand. These smaller establishments prioritize genuine hospitality and quality ingredients over elaborate presentation, creating dining experiences that feel personal rather than manufactured for tourists.

## Eco-Luxury with Character

For accommodations, Laluna stands out as a shining example of Grenada's hospitality philosophy. This boutique eco-resort masterfully combines environmental consciousness with genuine luxury, perched on hillsides that offer sweeping views of the Caribbean Sea. The property's restaurant serves an inventive fusion of Italian and Caribbean flavors, reflecting the island's diverse cultural influences while maintaining a commitment to sustainable practices. Rather than overwhelming guests with excess, Laluna and similar properties emphasize thoughtful design, natural beauty, and authentic connection to the local environment.

## The True Treasure: A Spice Island Legacy

While Grenada's dining and lodging options provide plenty of appeal, the island's most remarkable distinction lies elsewhere entirely. Grenada holds the extraordinary title of being the world's most concentrated producer of spices per square mile—an agricultural achievement that has earned it the nickname "The Spice Isle." Nutmeg, cinnamon, cloves, and cocoa thrive across the island's fertile volcanic soil, creating fragrant plantations that visitors can explore and experience firsthand.

This spice heritage isn't merely a historical footnote or marketing gimmick—it's woven into the daily rhythm of island life, influencing everything from local cuisine to the scented breezes that drift through the countryside. For travelers seeking something beyond typical beach vacation clichés, this agricultural legacy offers a genuine window into Grenada's identity and economy.

## An Alternative Caribbean Experience

Ultimately, Grenada positions itself as an antidote to the more flashy, overdeveloped Caribbean destinations that dominate travel brochures. Here, visitors discover that true luxury doesn't require ostentatious displays—it can be found in a perfectly prepared meal by the sea, a thoughtfully designed eco-resort with stunning views, and the simple pleasure of walking through spice plantations that have sustained this island community for generations. This combination of culinary authenticity, sustainable hospitality, and agricultural distinction makes Grenada a compelling choice for travelers seeking substance over spectacle.

# Coastal Living: Finding Peace by the Sea

There's something universally captivating about life along the coast. The rhythmic sound of waves, the salty breeze carrying hints of adventure, and the ever-changing horizon where sky meets sea create an environment unlike any other. Coastal living offers a unique blend of natural beauty and lifestyle benefits that continue to draw people to shorelines around the world.

## The Appeal of Coastal Communities

Living near the water fundamentally changes daily rhythms. Mornings often begin with watching the sunrise paint the sky in brilliant colors reflected across the water's surface. Evenings bring the ritual of sunset watching, a moment of collective pause that many coastal residents cherish. This connection to natural cycles fosters a slower, more mindful approach to life that contrasts sharply with landlocked urban existence.

The communities that develop along coastlines often share distinctive characteristics. Fishing villages transformed into charming towns, historic ports evolved into vibrant cities, and quiet beach communities all demonstrate how proximity to water shapes culture, architecture, and social patterns. Local economies frequently center around maritime industries, tourism, and hospitality, creating unique job opportunities tied directly to the sea.

## Health and Wellness Benefits

Research consistently shows that coastal living correlates with improved mental and physical wellbeing. The negative ions produced by crashing waves are believed to increase oxygen flow to the brain, potentially boosting mood and energy levels. Salt air has long been associated with respiratory benefits, while the simple act of walking on sand provides excellent low-impact exercise.

Beyond the physical advantages, there's an undeniable psychological comfort in ocean proximity. Studies in environmental psychology suggest that blue spaces—bodies of water—can reduce stress and anxiety similarly to how green spaces affect our mental state. The vastness of the ocean often provides perspective, helping people process emotions and find calm amid life's challenges.

## Challenges of Life by the Water

Despite its appeal, coastal living isn't without difficulties. Rising sea levels and increased storm intensity due to climate change pose real threats to coastal properties and infrastructure. Erosion continuously reshapes shorelines, sometimes claiming land that once seemed permanent. Insurance costs for coastal properties can be substantial, reflecting these environmental risks.

Additionally, the popularity of coastal areas often drives up real estate prices, making waterfront living increasingly exclusive. Tourist seasons bring both economic benefits and challenges, as year-round residents navigate crowded summers followed by quieter off-seasons that can strain local businesses.

## Sustainable Approaches to Coastal Development

As awareness of environmental challenges grows, many coastal communities are embracing sustainable development practices. This includes building with resilient materials, implementing better stormwater management, preserving natural barriers like dunes and wetlands, and adopting building codes that account for future climate scenarios.

Some regions are pioneering innovative solutions such as elevated construction, living shorelines that use natural elements to prevent erosion, and community-based conservation efforts that protect marine ecosystems while supporting human habitation.

## Conclusion

Coastal living represents a profound relationship between humans and the sea—one built on beauty, opportunity, and respect for nature's power. Whether drawn by the promise of daily sunrises over water, the rhythm of tides, or simply the desire to live somewhere that feels perpetually alive with movement and possibility, those who choose coastal life often speak of an irreplaceable connection to their surroundings. As we move forward, balancing the appeal of oceanside living with responsible environmental stewardship will be essential in preserving these treasured spaces for future generations.

# Grenada: The Spice of the Caribbean

*Where hidden coves, fragrant nutmeg groves, and unpretentious luxury create an island escape unlike any other*

---

There's a moment, driving the winding coastal road from Grenada's Maurice Bishop International Airport, when the scent hits you before the scenery does—warm, sweet, and earthy, like a spice cake pulled fresh from the oven. This is Grenada's calling card: the Isle of Spice, where nutmeg trees grow wild alongside cocoa pods and cinnamon bark, and where the pace of life still moves to the rhythm of the tides rather than the tourist season.

While its Caribbean neighbors have leaned hard into all-inclusive sprawl, Grenada has quietly remained something rarer—an island where you can still stumble upon a hidden black-sand beach with no one else on it, or share a rum punch with the fisherman who caught your dinner an hour earlier.

## Sleeping Barefoot at Laluna

Just south of the capital, St. George's, tucked into a private cove along Morne Rouge Bay, sixteen thatched-roof cottages sit scattered across a hillside like driftwood washed ashore. This is Laluna, the kind of place that doesn't advertise because it doesn't need to.

Built by an Italian design collective in the early 2000s, the resort has aged into something even better than trendy—it's become timeless. Balinese-inspired bungalows open directly onto a crescent of soft sand, each one privately positioned so you might not see another guest for your entire stay. There are no televisions, no keycards, no rigid dress codes. Just an open-air restaurant serving Italian-Caribbean fusion (the lobster ravioli, made with spiny lobster pulled from local waters that morning, is worth the trip alone), a spa built into the hillside, and a bar where the bartender remembers your drink order by day two.

Laluna isn't flashy. It's the anti-resort resort—proof that true luxury is often just space, quiet, and the sound of waves outside your door.

## Where the Locals Eat

Grenada's best meals rarely come with white tablecloths. In Gouyave, the island's fishing hub on the west coast, Friday nights mean **Fish Friday**, a street festival where vendors grill mahi-mahi, conch, and lambi (conch fritters) over open flames while steel pan music drifts through the crowd. Grab a plate, a Carib beer, and find a curb to sit on—it's the most authentic dinner party on the island.

In St. George's, seek out **BB's Crabback**, a modest restaurant run by chef Brian Benjamin that transforms the humble land crab into an elegant, spice-rubbed delicacy served in its own shell. For something more low-key, **De Big Fish** in the Carenage—the horseshoe harbor that forms the heart of the capital—serves grilled snapper with callaloo and provision (Grenada's answer to a root vegetable medley) at prices that feel like a rounding error.

Don't skip the rum shops, either. Places like **Belmont Estate**'s tasting room or the roadside stalls slinging Clarke's Court rum will teach you more about Grenadian culture in twenty minutes than any guidebook could.

## The Nutmeg That Built an Island

Grenada produces nearly 20% of the world's nutmeg supply, and the spice is stitched into everything here—the flag, the cuisine, even the local rum punches, which get a final grating of fresh nutmeg instead of the ground stuff from your pantry.

At the **Gouyave Nutmeg Processing Station**, a co-op that's operated since the 1940s, visitors can watch the entire process unfold: workers sorting nutmeg by hand, separating the mace (the lacy red covering) from the seed, and grading each nut by size and quality before it's shipped worldwide. The station took a direct hit from Hurricane Ivan in 2004, which wiped out nearly 90% of the island's nutmeg trees, but farmers replanted, and the industry has slowly, stubbornly recovered—a quiet testament to Grenadian resilience.

For a deeper dive, drive up into the hills to **Belmont Estate**, a working organic farm and heritage site where you can walk through cocoa and nutmeg groves, watch cocoa beans ferment and dry in the sun, and finish with a farm-to-table lunch featuring ingredients grown on-site.

## Beyond the Beach

Save an afternoon for **Concord Falls**, a series of three waterfalls tucked into the rainforest interior, or **Grand Etang National Park**, a volcanic crater lake ringed by mona monkeys and hiking trails. And don't miss the **Underwater Sculpture Park** off Molinere Bay—the world's first of its kind, where submerged concrete figures have become an artificial reef, now coated in coral and swarmed by parrotfish.

---

Grenada doesn't try to be the loudest island in the Caribbean. It doesn't need to be. What it offers instead is something increasingly rare: a place that still feels like a discovery, spice-scented and unhurried, exactly as it should be.

# Grenada Beyond the Beaches: Hidden Gems on the Spice Isle

Most travelers know Grenada for its powdery beaches and fragrant nutmeg plantations, but this small Caribbean island holds surprises for those willing to venture off the well-trodden path. Here's a look at three experiences that showcase a different side of Grenada.

## True Blue Bay: An Intimate Boutique Escape

Tucked along a quiet lagoon on the island's southern coast, **True Blue Bay Boutique Resort** offers something increasingly rare in the Caribbean: genuine intimacy without sacrificing style. With just a modest collection of rooms, suites, and cottages scattered across tropical gardens, the property feels more like a private retreat than a hotel.

The resort's design draws on local Caribbean aesthetics—colorful gingerbread-style architecture, hand-painted murals, and open-air spaces that invite the sea breeze in. Its floating waterfront restaurant, Dodgy Dock, has become something of a local institution, serving fresh seafood and Grenadian specialties while guests watch fishing boats drift by. Yoga sessions on the deck, sunset kayaking excursions, and a spa specializing in cocoa and nutmeg-infused treatments round out the experience.

What sets True Blue Bay apart is its commitment to sustainability and community—many ingredients come from local farms, and the resort actively supports Grenadian artisans and musicians.

## Grand Etang National Park: Rainforest Wonder

Just a 30-minute drive from the capital, St. George's, **Grand Etang National Park** feels like an entirely different world. Named for the crater lake at its center (a dormant volcano now filled with still, mysterious water), this rainforest reserve is Grenada's ecological heart.

Hiking trails wind through dense canopy alive with the calls of Mona monkeys, armadillos, and over 150 bird species. The moderate hike to Concord Falls or the more challenging trek up Mount Qua Qua rewards visitors with panoramic views across the island to the Caribbean Sea beyond. Morning visits are best—mist often rolls through the forest, giving the landscape an ethereal quality, and wildlife tends to be more active before midday heat sets in.

A visitor center near the lake offers context on the island's volcanic origins and rainforest ecology, making this an ideal stop for families and nature enthusiasts alike. Guides are readily available and highly recommended, both for safety and for their encyclopedic knowledge of medicinal plants and local folklore tied to the forest.

## Fish Friday in Gouyave: A Feast for the Senses

Every Friday evening, the fishing village of **Gouyave** on Grenada's western coast transforms into a sprawling open-air street party known as **Fish Friday**. What began as a modest community gathering has evolved into one of the island's most beloved weekly traditions, drawing locals and visitors alike.

Vendors line the streets grilling, frying, and stewing the day's catch—think garlic butter lobster, spicy conch, grilled mahi-mahi, and fried shark, all paired with sides like roasted breadfruit, callaloo, and coconut bread. The air fills with reggae and soca music, rum punch flows freely, and the entire village takes on the atmosphere of a joyful, informal carnival.

Arrive hungry and with cash in hand—most stalls are small, family-run operations, and prices are refreshingly affordable. Come early evening to beat the crowds, though the energy builds as the night goes on.

---

## Practical Booking Information

**True Blue Bay Boutique Resort**
Book directly through the resort's website (truebluebay.com) or via major booking platforms. Rates vary seasonally; the dry season (December–April) commands premium pricing, while summer months offer better value. Airport transfers can typically be arranged through the resort.

**Grand Etang National Park**
Entry requires a small fee, payable at the visitor center. Guided hikes can be booked through local tour operators in St. George's or arranged through your accommodation. No advance reservation is necessary, though hiring a guide in advance is wise during peak season.

**Fish Friday, Gouyave**
No reservations needed—simply show up between 6 and 9 pm on Friday evenings. Many tour companies and hotels, including True Blue Bay, offer organized transport and small-group excursions if you'd prefer not to navigate the 45-minute drive from St. George's independently.

*Best time to visit Grenada overall: December through April offers the driest, most temperate weather, though the island's rainforest interior stays lush and hike-worthy year-round.*

# Grenada: The Other Caribbean

There's a particular shade of green that exists only in Grenada—a deep, saturated emerald that coats the mountains rolling down to meet an impossibly turquoise sea. This is the Caribbean before the crowds, before the cruise ship terminals and duty-free megaplexes turned so much of the region into a shopping mall with a beach view. Grenada, tucked into the southeastern corner of the Lesser Antilles, has quietly resisted that fate. Call it the other Caribbean: slower, wilder, and infinitely more fragrant.

## A Different Kind of Beautiful

Fly into Maurice Bishop International and the descent alone tells you something is different here. Rainforest-cloaked peaks rise from the interior like green cathedrals, and waterfalls—more than a dozen worth seeking out—tumble through the hills toward the coast. Grand Etang National Park, centered on a volcanic crater lake, offers hiking trails thick with mona monkeys, armadillos, and birdsong instead of souvenir stands.

The coastline does its part too. Grand Anse Beach delivers the two-mile stretch of powder-soft sand that postcards promise, but it's the smaller, harder-to-reach coves—Bathway Beach on the wild Atlantic side, or the volcanic black sand at Pearls—that reward the traveler willing to rent a car and wander. Underwater, Grenada holds its own surprise: an actual sculpture park submerged off the coast, where concrete figures slowly become part of the reef, growing coral for skin.

## Laluna: Barefoot Luxury, Reimagined

If Grenada has a signature address, it's Laluna, a boutique eco-resort tucked into a private cove on the island's southwestern edge. Built by an Italian design team with an eye for restraint rather than spectacle, Laluna consists of just sixteen cottages, each with its own plunge pool, scattered along a hillside above a beach so private it feels invented.

The aesthetic here is barefoot-chic: thatched roofs, Balinese-inspired furnishings, sea-facing verandas where breakfast arrives without you ever having to ask. But the real luxury is restraint. There's no oversized lobby, no relentless activities board—just space to disappear into hammocks strung between palms, a spa built into the hillside, and a restaurant serving Mediterranean-Caribbean fusion using produce grown a few miles up the road. Solar power and rainwater harvesting run quietly in the background, proof that eco-conscious doesn't have to mean roughing it. Laluna doesn't so much compete with the Caribbean's grand resorts as opt out of that conversation entirely.

## The Island That Smells Like Nutmeg

Long before "farm-to-table" was a marketing phrase, Grenada was living it—just with spices instead of vegetables. Known for centuries as the Spice Isle, Grenada produces nearly forty percent of the world's nutmeg, along with cloves, cinnamon, turmeric, and cocoa that finds its way into some of the world's most sought-after single-origin chocolate bars.

Drive inland and the evidence is everywhere: nutmeg trees heavy with fruit, drying sheds with slatted roofs designed to let the Caribbean sun do the work, roadside stands selling mace and cinnamon bark wrapped in banana leaf. At the Gouyave Nutmeg Processing Station, workers still sort spices by hand, grading them by size and quality in a process that hasn't changed much since the 1800s—a rhythm interrupted only briefly in 2004, when Hurricane Ivan flattened much of the nutmeg industry. The trees have since regrown, and with them, the island's signature scent: warm, woody, and faintly sweet, drifting through market stalls in St. George's and kitchens across the island alike.

This is a place where the landscape and the economy and the cuisine are the same story, told in cinnamon and clove.

---

## 🌴 ISLAND INFO

**Getting There:** Direct flights from New York, Miami, and Toronto; connections available via Barbados, Trinidad, or St. Lucia.

**Best Time to Visit:** December through May for dry season; visit in August for the Spicemas Carnival, one of the Caribbean's most vibrant celebrations.

**Currency:** Eastern Caribbean Dollar (EC$); US dollars widely accepted.

**Where to Stay:** Laluna (boutique/eco-luxury); Spice Island Beach Resort (beachfront luxury); True Blue Bay Resort (family-friendly, mid-range).

**Don't Miss:** Grand Etang National Park, the Underwater Sculpture Park at Molinere Bay, Gouyave Nutmeg Processing Station, River Antoine Rum Distillery (still water-wheel powered).

**Local Flavor:** Try "oil down," Grenada's national dish—breadfruit, salted meat, and callaloo stewed in coconut milk—and don't leave without a jar of local nutmeg syrup.

**Language:** English (official), with Grenadian Creole widely spoken.

**Pro Tip:** Rent a car for at least one day. Grenada's interior roads are winding but manageable, and the reward—hidden waterfalls, spice estates, mountain viewpoints—is worth the slow pace.

# Grenada's Secret Coast: Where the Spice Island Serves Its Best

*A journey through hidden hillsides, rum-soaked evenings, and the freshest catch in the Caribbean*

---

There's a particular quality of light that falls across Grenada in the late afternoon—amber and unhurried, filtering through nutmeg trees before settling onto beaches that still feel like discoveries rather than destinations. This is the Spice Island, where cinnamon bark peels in roadside markets and the scent of cocoa drying on tarps drifts through open-air taxis. But Grenada's real magic reveals itself after dark, when the island's dining and lodging scene comes alive with an intimacy that larger Caribbean destinations have long since traded away.

## An Evening at Little Dipper

Tucked along the shoreline with barely a sign to announce it, **Little Dipper** feels less like a restaurant and more like a dinner party thrown by someone with impeccable taste and a direct line to the fishing boats. Candlelit tables spill toward the sand, and the menu changes with what came in that morning—perhaps a peppery callaloo soup, followed by grilled mahi-mahi finished with tamarind glaze and a scatter of micro greens grown just up the hill.

The wine list is surprisingly deep for such an unassuming spot, and the service moves at the pace of the tide: unhurried, attentive, never rushed. Reservations are essential, particularly during the December-to-April high season, as tables rarely exceed a dozen.

*Little Dipper Restaurant, True Blue Bay, St. George's | +1 (473) 444-2000 | Reservations recommended, dinner only*

## Sleeping Among the Trees at Laluna

If Grenada has a definitive answer to barefoot luxury, it's **Laluna**, an Italian-designed enclave of sixteen cottages scattered across a jungled hillside above Morne Rouge Bay. Each bungalow is its own private world—thatched roofs, indoor-outdoor bathrooms, and a plunge pool positioned to catch the sunset without another soul in view.

Mornings here begin with fruit plucked that day and coffee delivered to your veranda by staff who seem to materialize exactly when needed and vanish just as gracefully otherwise. The beach below is a private half-moon of pale sand, shared only with fellow guests and the occasional heron. It's the kind of place that ruins you for ordinary hotels.

*Laluna, Morne Rouge Bay, St. George's | +1 (473) 439-0001 | lalunahotel.com | Cottages from $450/night*

## Into the Rainforest: Grand Etang

No visit to Grenada is complete without ascending into **Grand Etang National Park**, where a volcanic crater lake sits mirror-still at 1,740 feet, ringed by rainforest thick with mona monkeys and armored ground lizards. The hiking trails here range from a gentle twenty-minute loop around the lake to the more demanding trek up Mount Qua Qua, where clouds roll through the canopy like slow-motion weather systems.

Guides—easily arranged through the visitor center—point out the medicinal bark trees and wild nutmeg that first drew colonial fortune-seekers to this island centuries ago. Pack a light rainproof layer; the interior climate shifts quickly, and afternoon showers are as reliable as the sunrise.

*Grand Etang National Park & Forest Reserve, Interior Grenada | +1 (473) 440-6160 | Visitor center open daily 8:30am–4pm | Entry $2 USD*

## Fish Friday in Gouyave

But for the island's most joyful culinary tradition, drive north to the fishing town of Gouyave on a Friday evening, when the entire main street transforms into **Fish Fridays**—a rollicking, generations-old street festival built entirely around the catch. Vendors line the road with grills smoking, frying oil popping, and speakers thumping soca into the salt air.

Order the grilled snapper wrapped in foil with garlic butter, or the lambi (conch) souse, ladled from enormous pots into styrofoam bowls. Wash it down with a Carib beer or a rum punch poured a little heavier than you'd expect. Locals dance in the street; visitors are pulled in without much resistance required. It's messy, loud, and unmissable—the kind of evening that makes you understand why people fall for this island and never quite leave.

*Fish Friday, Gouyave, St. John Parish | Fridays, 6pm–late | Cash only, no reservations needed*

---

*For general Grenada tourism information, contact the Grenada Tourism Authority at +1 (473) 440-2279 or visit puregrenada.com*

# The Island That Smells Like Christmas: Discovering Grenada's Quiet Magic

The first thing you notice isn't the turquoise water lapping against volcanic black sand, or the emerald hills rolling toward the clouds. It's the smell—warm, sweet, and unmistakably like your grandmother's kitchen during the holidays. This is Grenada, the Caribbean's best-kept secret, where nutmeg trees outnumber tourists and the pace of life moves to the rhythm of steel drums drifting from some unseen rum shop.

## Where the Spice Grows Wild

Grenada earned its nickname—the "Spice Isle"—honestly. Drive the winding roads through the interior and you'll pass nutmeg groves so dense the air itself seems perfumed. At the **Gouyave Nutmeg Processing Station**, a rust-tinged, century-old building where workers still sort nutmeg by hand, the scent hits you before you even step through the door: earthy, warm, faintly peppery. Baskets of the wrinkled brown seeds spill across wooden tables, their crimson mace coverings peeled away and dried separately.

Ask a local how they take their rum, and they'll likely mention a fresh grate of nutmeg on top—a small ritual that turns any evening into something sacred.

## Luxury That Doesn't Shout

Unlike its flashier Caribbean cousins, Grenada's luxury whispers rather than announces itself. At **Silversands Grenada**, an infinity pool—the longest in the Caribbean—stretches toward Grand Anse Beach, its water so still at dawn it mirrors the sky perfectly. Rooms here feel like private sanctuaries: polished concrete floors, floor-to-ceiling windows, and outdoor rain showers where you can hear the surf while lathering in locally-made cocoa soap.

Further south, **Mount Cinnamon Resort** clings to a hillside above Grand Anse, its Caribbean-colonial cottages draped in bougainvillea. Evenings here mean rum punch on your private deck, watching fishing boats bob against a sky bruised purple and orange, while the scent of someone's evening curry drifts up from the beach bars below.

## A Table Set With the Whole Island

If you time your visit right, you'll stumble into Grenada's food festival season—an unpretentious, joyful celebration of everything the island grows and cooks. The **Grenada Chocolate Festival** (held each May) transforms the town of St. George's into an open-air tasting room, where local chocolatiers—working with beans grown just miles away—hand out squares of dark, smoky chocolate alongside cocoa tea spiced with cinnamon and, naturally, nutmeg.

Don't miss **Fish Friday** in Gouyave, a weekly street festival rather than an annual one, where fishermen's wives grill lambi (conch), fry saltfish fritters, and stew callaloo in giant pots along the roadside. Plastic tables spill onto the street, strangers become friends over shared plates, and a live band always seems to materialize by 9 p.m.

## The Rhythm of the Rest of the Day

Beyond the resorts and festivals, Grenada rewards slow mornings. Hike to **Seven Sisters Falls** in Grand Etang National Rainforest, where waterfalls cascade through jungle so thick with green it feels prehistoric. Locals will urge you to jump from the rocks into cold, clear pools below—an invitation you should absolutely accept.

Or spend an afternoon at **River Antoine Rum Distillery**, still powered by a 200-year-old waterwheel, where the rum is bottled at a startling 75% proof and workers will pour you a taste straight from the barrel.

---

## Plan Your Trip

**Getting There:** Direct flights available from Miami, New York, and Toronto to Maurice Bishop International Airport (GND).

**Where to Stay:**
- Silversands Grenada — from $650/night (silversandsgrenada.com)
- Mount Cinnamon Resort — from $420/night (mountcinnamongrenada.com)
- True Blue Bay Boutique Resort — from $280/night, family-friendly (truebluebay.com)

**Festivals to Plan Around:**
- Grenada Chocolate Festival — mid-May annually (grenadachocolatefest.com)
- Fish Friday, Gouyave — every Friday evening, free to attend
- Grenada Spice Mas Carnival — August

**Tourism Information:**
Grenada Tourism Authority
Phone: +1 (473) 440-2001
Website: puregrenada.com

**Best Time to Visit:** December through May, dry season, avoiding hurricane risk and peak humidity.

*Grenada doesn't try to impress you. It simply is what it is—unhurried, fragrant, and generous—and somehow, that's far more seductive than anywhere trying too hard to earn your attention.*
